title: Jahanshah Qaraqoyunlu Manuscript Witness Census

authors.name: Kazemipourleilabadi, Negar
authors.affiliation: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Department of Art History

intro: This dataset records manuscript witnesses for the dispersed Dīvān tradition of Jahanshah Qaraqoyunlu (d. 872 AH / 1467 CE; pen name Ḥaqīqī / Hakîkî). It also documents an LLM-assisted search workflow for building a census across inconsistent multilingual catalogues, printed references, private and community archives, blocked or non-searchable portals, and lost or unlocated reports.
search_key_summary: It includes a 257-string search-key matrix: 99 base author/title/context/scribe/Nesimi strings, 106 additional script-family variants, 12 South Asian homonym-disambiguation queries, and 40 Alevi-community route/contact terms. The matrix covers 14 language/script or orthographic traditions: modern Latin, Turkish/Ottoman Turkish, French and German Orientalist forms, Persian/Arabic-script forms, Russian Cyrillic, Azerbaijani Latin/Cyrillic, Georgian, Uzbek Latin/Cyrillic, Tajik Cyrillic, Devanagari, and Urdu nastaliq. The release also includes 5 tezkire or tezkire-adjacent reference extracts and 5 research-log extracts on Hakîkî where available.
alevi_summary: The Alevi shrine corpus records eleven published ghazals from Anatolian and Iranian Azerbaijani Ocak traditions that are absent from the institutional editions checked here. It also reports a complete, unphotographed divan codex in the Ilkhchi archive.
methodology_summary: The deposit includes 37 indexed search-session and action records, the search-key matrix, search-surface counting rules, false-positive classifications, and a recovery agenda for blocked, private, and on-site manuscript sources. LLM tools assisted search-term expansion, catalogue-variant reconciliation, homonym checking, false-positive logging, and access-gap mapping; witness classifications and attribution decisions remain source-based and human-reviewed. Known failure modes for this use case include over-definitive coverage claims, wrong shelfmarks for real manuscripts, and hallucinated bibliographic entries; human source review and cross-model LLM review were used to mitigate those risks before public claims were retained.
